extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, philosophy of science researchers, and graduate students interested in explanation in mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-level treatment distinguishing kinds of mathematical explanation (intra-mathematical vs extra-mathematical) and classifying explanatory demonstrations (axiomatic/analytic, top-down/bottom-up), arguing about which kinds genuinely provide explanation and understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical explanations of mathematical facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Two different kinds of mathematical explanations can be distinguished: mathematical explanations of mathematical facts; the chapter argues that there are mathematical explanations of mathematical facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion identifies explanations that operate within mathematics itself (intra-mathematical). The chapter treats these as genuine explanatory relations that can yield understanding of mathematical truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical explanations of empirical facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Two different kinds of mathematical explanations can be distinguished: mathematical explanations of empirical facts; the chapter argues that there are no mathematical explanations of empirical facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion concerns attempts to use mathematics to explain empirical phenomena (extra-mathematical explanations). The chapter's position is that such explanations are illusory; they do not constitute genuine mathematical explanations of empirical facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intra-mathematical explanations
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers explanations that relate mathematical facts to other mathematical facts or structures. Evaluative focus: whether the account genuinely explains within the conceptual/mathematical framework and contributes to mathematical understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extra-mathematical explanations
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers claims that mathematics explains non-mathematical (empirical) phenomena. The chapter labels these as illusory and treats their purported explanatory role skeptically; evaluators should check whether the purported explanation bridges the gap between mathematical form and empirical causal/ontological facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory axiomatic demonstration
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A class of mathematical demonstration characterized by appeal to axioms/axiomatic structure; evaluative attention on whether the axiomatic argument illuminates why a result holds (not merely that it holds). Examples and distinctions from other demonstration types are discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory analytic demonstration
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A class of demonstration relying on analytic or conceptual analysis; evaluative focus is on whether the analytic route provides explanatory insight and contributes to understanding, compared to axiomatic or other proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Top-down explanatory demonstration
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrations that derive specific results from higher-level principles or structures; evaluative criteria include the extent to which the top-level principles legitimately account for the phenomenon and increase explanatory generality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bottom-up explanatory demonstration
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrations that build explanation from particular cases or constructions toward general results; evaluative focus on whether such constructions reveal the mechanisms or reasons for a theorem, thereby contributing to understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory demonstration and understanding
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addresses the link between demonstration types and the kind/degree of understanding they deliver. Evaluation should consider whether a proof/demonstration provides genuine understanding (not merely justification), and how different explanatory forms compare in this respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illusoriness of extra-mathematical explanations
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter explicitly raises the idea that extra-mathematical explanations (mathematics explaining empirical facts) are illusory. As a criterion, this invites scrutiny of purported cases: do they really explain the empirical fact, or do they only offer formal representation without genuine explanatory power?
